clue.text: Navy shop supplying country music

blocks.note: navy is a dark shade of blue
to shop someone is to inform on them, in British slang to grass

explanation.surface: A naval store sells records of country and western songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'shop' and 'grass' are British slang for informing on someone to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluegrass is a style of American folk music from Kentucky, played on banjo and fiddle.

clue.text: Brook's on time but gets fired

blocks.note: a burn is a Scottish word for a small stream
T is the standard abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone called Brook is punctual yet still loses their job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brook' looks like a person's name; it is a stream, which in Scotland and northern England is called a burn.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fired in a kiln or oven has been scorched, as in pottery or bricks that were burnt.

clue.text: Do without strong ointment

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the word for strong is taken away from the first word

blocks.note: a do is a party or social event
F is forte, the musical marking for loud or strong

explanation.surface: Instruction to manage without a powerful medicinal cream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is not a verb here but a noun, a party: FUNCTION, from which F (forte) is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Unction is an archaic or religious word for anointing oil or a soothing salve applied to the skin.

clue.text: One who's certain to pass on £1001

definitions.text: One who's certain to pass on

blocks.note: a G or grand is slang for a thousand pounds
a oner is British slang for a single pound, the remaining one of the sum

explanation.surface: Someone sure to die leaves a bequest of one thousand and one pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The sum splits as a thousand plus one: G (a grand) and ONER (an old slang name for a pound note).
explanation.definitionFit: A goner is a person or thing doomed, beyond help, about to die.

clue.text: Tall bats on the way out – nothing more to add

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so the word before it is jumbled up

blocks.note: taken as written
something on the way out is ageing or outdated

explanation.surface: Tall cricket bats are being phased out, and that is the whole story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like cricket bats or flying mammals; here it is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: All told means in total, once everything is counted, so the sum is complete with no further items.

clue.text: Tried dancing in fire to create a diversion

indicators.note: dancing letters move about and end up in a new order
in places the jumbled word inside the word for fire

blocks.note: taken as written
to fire someone is to sack them

explanation.surface: Someone attempted a dance during a blaze to distract onlookers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' suggests flames, but it means dismiss from a job: SACK, split around the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To sidetrack is to divert attention or a person from the main issue, as a distraction does.

clue.text: Get aggressively physical when criminal Ray dips into till

indicators.note: criminal suggests something bent or crooked, so the name is twisted
dipping into something means going inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
to till the soil is to plough it

explanation.surface: A crook named Ray steals from the cash register, and things turn violent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Till' looks like a cash register, which suits the criminal story; it is the farming verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To play rough is to use excessive force or violence in a game or contest.

clue.text: Paid player to ache and stretch

blocks.note: a professional is a player who is paid
to ache for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: A professional sportsman suffers aches and does his stretches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ache' and 'stretch' look like gym talk; ache means yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: To prolong something is to extend it in time, lengthening its duration.

clue.text: Government system one mixed up with Sparta

indicators.note: mixed letters are stirred together into a fresh order

blocks.note: one is the article a
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An administrative system confused with that of ancient Sparta.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed up' reads as a single anagram signal, but only 'mixed' is; the UP goes into the anagram with the A and SPARTA.
explanation.definitionFit: The apparatus of state is the organised machinery or structure through which a government operates.

clue.text: Go east in Northern Line for a nutty filling

indicators.note: in puts the direction letter inside the pair of letters that follows

blocks.note: to have a go at something is to have a crack at it
N for northern and L for line
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Travelling east on the London Underground's Northern Line in search of a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northern Line' is a London Tube line, but here it is just two abbreviations, N and L.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracknel is a brittle confection of nuts set in caramel, used as a centre in chocolates.

clue.text: Limp extremely drunkenly, nursing bad back

indicators.note: extremely points to the two extremes, the outermost letters of the next word
back means the word for bad is read in the opposite direction
nursing means holding something close, so one piece cradles another

blocks.note: first and last letters only
poor quality is bad

explanation.surface: Someone hobbles along drunk while nursing a sore back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad back' reads as an injury; 'back' signals a turnaround of the word for bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Droopy means hanging down limply, sagging without stiffness or vigour.

clue.text: English climber's foot caught in level rope ladder

indicators.note: the foot of a word is its bottom or final letter
caught in means trapped inside the word for level

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
last letter only
a tier is a level or layer

explanation.surface: An English mountaineer gets a foot tangled in a rope ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down-clue sense the foot of a word is its last letter, here the end of 'climber'.
explanation.definitionFit: An etrier is a short rope ladder with a few rungs, used by climbers in aid climbing.

clue.text: Disallowed opportunities, not having a roof over your head?

definitions.text: not having a roof over your head?

blocks.note: something ruled out is disallowed
opportunities are doors, as in doors opening for someone

explanation.surface: A homeless person is denied chances in life.
explanation.definitionFit: Being outside in the open air means there is no ceiling or shelter above you, hence the playful question mark.

clue.text: Christmas-time drink, say, before flipping dinner alert?

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it round end to end

blocks.note: e.g. means for example, which is what say means here
a gong is struck to call people to dinner

explanation.surface: A seasonal drink is served before the dinner bell is impatiently sounded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word before 'dinner alert'; it is the turnaround signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a rich drink of eggs, milk, sugar and often spirits, traditionally served over Christmas.

clue.text: Bizarre Greek quotes about conserving energy

indicators.note: about means turned around and scattered, so these letters are rearranged
conserving means keeping something safe within, so the scrambled word holds the letter

blocks.note: Gr is the abbreviation for Greek
taken as written
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: Odd lines from a Greek writer that touch on keeping energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'on the subject of'; it signals scrambling the word after Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Grotesque describes something weird, distorted or fantastically strange, much as bizarre does.

clue.text: Topping contractor, this boss?

blocks.note: surface reading: an excellent builder or tradesman who takes on contracts
setter's reading: the head of a Mafia family, who hands out contracts to kill, topping being slang for killing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' reads as excellent and 'contractor' as a builder; in criminal slang to top someone is to kill them, and a contract is an order for a killing.
explanation.definitionFit: The godfather is the head of a Mafia family, the crime boss who orders murders.

clue.text: Currently cold, needing doctor – anything – at end of day

indicators.note: the end of a word is its closing letter, so only that one is taken

blocks.note: Dr is the abbreviation for doctor
aught is an old word for anything
last letter only

explanation.surface: Someone is feeling chilly at the moment and wants a doctor of any kind by evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currently' looks like 'at present', but it means by a current of air.
explanation.definitionFit: A draughty room is cold because currents of air blow through it.

clue.text: Tilting executed by quirky spoiled duke

indicators.note: quirky means odd and unconventional, so the next word's letters are put into an odd order

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for duke

explanation.surface: A jousting contest carried out by an eccentric, pampered aristocrat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tilting' suggests jousting, which suits a duke; it is the definition, meaning leaning to one side.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lopsided is uneven, leaning or tipped more to one side than the other.

clue.text: Reverse bet's off – in the bag

indicators.note: off means gone wrong or awry, so those letters are disordered
in places the scrambled word inside the word for bag

blocks.note: taken as written
a sack is a large bag

explanation.surface: A wager is cancelled, though the result seemed already in the bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the bag' reads as the idiom for certain to be won; it is literal here.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverse is a setback, a defeat or check to progress.

clue.text: Candy twists containing note: 'full of beans'

indicators.note: twists means the letters before it are wrung into a new order
containing means the jumbled letters hold the musical syllable inside

blocks.note: taken as written
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Twisted sweets come with a label saying they are full of energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Candy twists' look like a kind of sweet; 'twists' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone full of beans is lively and energetic, which is what dynamic means.

clue.text: Scupper King and I? Nonsense!

blocks.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
taken as written
bosh is an old word for nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses the musical The King and I as rubbish and wants it sunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King and I' looks like the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical; the words are taken separately.
explanation.definitionFit: To put the kibosh on something is to scupper it, bringing a plan to an end.

clue.text: Out of control horse gobbling small pillow?

indicators.note: gobbling means swallowing, so the small letter ends up inside

blocks.note: a bolter is a horse that runs off out of control
S is the abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A runaway horse wolfs down a little cushion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of control' looks like an anagram signal; it is part of the description of the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A bolster is a long, firm pillow placed across the head of a bed.

clue.text: Check on melody

blocks.note: re means on or concerning
a strain is a tune or snatch of melody

explanation.surface: An instruction to verify a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: To check something is to hold it back or curb it, the same as restraining it.

clue.text: Like Laurel is Hardy, to some extent?

indicators.note: to some extent means only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: Comparing Laurel to Hardy, the famous comedy double act.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurel and Hardy were a classic film comedy pair; 'Like' looks like a comparison but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To relish something is to enjoy it greatly, to like it.

clue.text: See 6 Across
Lace from southern Lakeland mountain

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for southern
in the Lake District a pike is a peaked hill, as in Scafell Pike

explanation.surface: Lace made in the southern part of the Lake District mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: Lakeland is the English Lake District, where many summits are called pikes.
explanation.definitionFit: To lace a drink is to spike it, adding alcohol or a drug secretly.

clue.text: Pulp, Queen united in band

indicators.note: in places the two letters inside the word for band

blocks.note: Q is the abbreviation for queen
U stands for united, as in football club names
a sash is a band of cloth worn round the waist or over the shoulder

explanation.surface: Britpop band Pulp and rock band Queen join forces.
explanation.walkthrough: Pulp and Queen are both British rock bands, so 'band' looks like a music group; it is a strip of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: To pulp something is to crush it to a soft mass, which is to squash it.

clue.text: Horse has one in heap

blocks.note: a mount is a horse for riding
one is the article a
taken as written

explanation.surface: A horse is buried in a big pile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is not a container signal here; it goes straight into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mountain of something, such as paperwork or washing, is a very large pile of it.

clue.text: Turn over board to see gander

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end

blocks.note: board and keep both mean food and lodging, as in earning your keep

explanation.surface: Flip a board over to have a look underneath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gander' looks like a male goose; to take a gander is British slang for to take a look.
explanation.definitionFit: A gander is informal for a quick look, the same as a peek.

clue.text: Nothing in research involved a runner

indicators.note: in places the letter for nothing within the next word
involved means intricately tangled, so all the letters are jumbled together

blocks.note: O looks like zero, nothing
taken as written

explanation.surface: No research was done on a competitor in the race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A runner' could be an athlete; in racing a runner is any horse taking part.
explanation.definitionFit: A racehorse entered in a race is called a runner by bookmakers and racing commentators.
